newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl coalition shows unity ahead of tax debate.
newsitem.headline: Kohl coalition shows unity ahead of tax debate.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition put on a show of unity ahead of what was set to be a bruising parliamentary debate on German tax reforms which have been blocked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
Sources in Kohl's three-party alliance said they had agreed to make a cut in an income tax surcharge next year -- whether or not Finance Minister Theo Waigel's main tax reform survives.
The deal meets demands by junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) to cut the solidarity surcharge by two points to 5.5 percent from the start of next year.

Waigel and other leaders from the Christian Democrat (CDU) wing of the Kohl government had hesitated, fearing that a cut could rip a new hole in state finances as Germany struggles to keep borrowing under control for Europe's single currency.

But they appeared to back down for the sake of government unity over an issue which has in the past threatened to break Kohl's government, in power since 1982. "Our intention is clear," one coalition source said.
Cutting the "soli", an unpopular levy raised to finance economic regeneration in eastern Germany, would cost around seven billion marks ($3.8 billion).

Government sources said proposals were being discussed to cover the cost of the reduction and ensure that Bonn sticks to the Maastricht treaty budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product next year.

While the government resolved its differences there was no sign the SPD was prepared to give up its opposition to Waigel's plan to slash 30 billion marks in taxes which it blocked last week in parliament's mediation committee.

Leaders of the SPD, which can veto tax changes through the party's majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, said a debate on the tax reforms in the lower house would not change their position.

Finance spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier told German Radio that the two sides were still "miles apart" on tax policy and said the best solution would be to bring forward general elections due to be held in September 1998.
"I don't think that we should continue this discussion for another 14 months," she said. "Let's have elections now so that each side can put its case to the voters."
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said it was a waste of time and money to interrupt the summer recess to debate reforms which have no chance of becoming law.
And he said that convening a second round of parliament's mediation process would not lead to a cross-party deal on tax reforms.

"This special session costs a lot of money and the result is already clear: the mediation process will be restarted, and as far as I'm concerned, we could do without it," he told Southwest German Radio.

Kohl's slim Bundestag majority is expected to bounce the tax reform back to the upper house, which will reject it when it meets in September. That will lead to a second round of parliamentary mediation.
The governing side will also reject SPD proposals for a two-point cut in labour insurance charges aimed at reducing the cost of labour and easing job creation.
But a cross-party deal struck in the mediation committee last week to abolish a capital trading tax on companies should be rubber-stamped by the Bundestag.
